title: Allocation decisions are made by an off-chain planner; the on-chain contracts only bound what it may do
content:
A.6.1.1.5.2.6.1.2.2.1.1.2 defines the Relayer as "the address for the Obex Liquidity Layer **ALM Planner off-chain system** that calls functions on `Controller` contracts to perform actions on behalf of the `ALMProxy` contract." The `ALM_CONTROLLER_ROLE` in turn "can call the `call` functions on the `ALMProxy` contract and update `RateLimits`," and controller contracts "are accessed and modified via the Relayer Role" (A.6.1.1.5.2.6.1.2.2.1.1.3).

The division of labour is clean. Strategy — how much USDS to mint, which vault to enter, when to rotate — lives off-chain in a planner that can hold market data, models and human judgement. The contracts hold none of that; every function description in this chunk follows the same shape: verify the caller's role, check the rate limit, execute, emit.

This is what makes the guardrails credible without making the system rigid. Encoding allocation strategy on-chain would freeze it; encoding only constraints leaves strategy free to evolve while keeping the worst case bounded regardless of what the planner decides — including if the planner is wrong, buggy, or compromised.

It also locates the real trust boundary. The Atlas documents the contracts exhaustively — every function signature, every revert condition — while the planner that actually decides is described in a single clause. A reader auditing this system can verify the *bounds* completely from the Artifact and the chain, and can verify the *decisions* not at all. That is a deliberate allocation of verifiability, and A.6.1.1.5.2.6.1.2.3 confirms the gap is known: "In the future, additional logic will be added herein regarding the strategy by which capital is allocated between different Instances."
description: The RELAYER_ROLE is held by the ALM Planner off-chain system, so the chain never chooses where capital goes — it enforces rate limits and venue permissions on choices made elsewhere.
